lessons.title: Class Declarations, Constructors & Instantiation
lessons.description: ES6 classes provide a clean syntax for creating objects with shared methods — syntactic sugar over prototypes.

sections.heading: What is a class?
paragraphs: A class is a blueprint for creating objects. It defines properties and methods that all instances share. Under the hood, classes use prototypes — but the syntax is much cleaner.
list: Declare with class ClassName { }
The constructor() method runs when you create a new instance with new
Instance methods are defined directly in the class body
Use new ClassName() to create instances

codeExamples.heading: Basic class declaration
explanation: class User defines a blueprint for creating user objects.
greet() is a method shared by all User instances.
new User() creates a fresh instance and calls the constructor.

practice.task: Create a Car class with make, model and year properties. Add a describe() method that returns a formatted string.
hints: Use constructor(make, model, year) to set properties.
Create an instance: let car = new Car("Toyota", "Camry", 2024).

keyTakeaways: Classes are blueprints for creating objects with shared methods.
The constructor() method runs when you create a new instance.
All instances share the same methods — efficient memory usage.
ES6 classes are syntactic sugar over prototype-based inheritance.
lessons.challenge: Create a BankAccount class with deposit, withdraw and getBalance methods. Test with multiple accounts.

lessons.title: Instance Methods, Getters, Setters & Static Methods
lessons.description: Classes support computed properties (getters/setters) and class-level methods (static).

sections.heading: Getters and setters
list: get propertyName() — runs when you access the property
set propertyName(value) — runs when you assign to the property
Let you add validation or computed values to properties
Access like normal properties: obj.name, not obj.name()

sections.heading: Static methods
list: static methodName() — called on the class itself, not instances
Use for utility functions related to the class
Cannot access this — they don't have an instance

codeExamples.heading: Getters, setters and static methods
explanation: Getters compute values on access — no parentheses needed.
Setters let you validate or transform data before storing it.
Static methods are called on the class: Temperature.fromFahrenheit().
The convention for internal storage is _propertyName.

practice.task: Create a Rectangle class with width and height. Add getters for area and perimeter. Add a static method that creates a square from a single side length.
hints: Static: static square(side) { return new Rectangle(side, side); }.

keyTakeaways: Getters and setters let you add computed properties with custom logic.
Static methods are called on the class itself, not on instances.
Getters/setters use the same syntax as property access — no parentheses.
Static methods are perfect for factory functions and utility methods.
lessons.challenge: Build a Queue class with enqueue, dequeue, peek (getter), and a static fromArray() method.

lessons.title: Private Class Fields (#private) & Static Blocks
lessons.description: True private fields with # prefix and static initialization blocks for class-level setup.

sections.heading: Private fields with #
paragraphs: ES2022 introduced truly private class fields using the # prefix. These are completely inaccessible from outside the class — even Object.keys() can't see them.
list: Declare with #fieldName in the class body
Accessible only inside the class methods
Not visible on the instance or through Object.keys()
The strongest encapsulation JavaScript offers

sections.heading: Static blocks
list: static { } runs once when the class is first loaded
Used for complex static initialization that can't be done in one line
Can access private static fields
Multiple static blocks run in order

codeExamples.heading: Private fields and static blocks
explanation: #balance is truly private — it cannot be accessed from outside the class.
The balance getter provides read-only access without exposing the raw field.
Private fields enforce encapsulation at the language level.
The # is part of the field name — #x and x are different fields.

practice.task: Create a class with a private field #count. Add public methods to increment, decrement and get the count. Verify the field is inaccessible from outside.

keyTakeaways: # prefix creates truly private fields — inaccessible from outside the class.
Private fields enforce encapsulation at the language level.
Static blocks run once at class load time for complex static initialization.
Use private fields for sensitive data like passwords, balances and internal state.
lessons.challenge: Build a Timer class with private fields for start time and elapsed time. Add methods for start, stop and a getter for the formatted elapsed time.

lessons.title: Inheritance Patterns: extends, super, and Method Overriding
lessons.description: Create class hierarchies with extends and override parent methods with your own implementations.

sections.heading: Class inheritance
list: class Child extends Parent — Child inherits all methods from Parent
super() in the constructor calls the parent's constructor (required before using this)
super.method() calls the parent's version of a method
Override by redefining the method in the child class

codeExamples.heading: Class inheritance with extends and super
explanation: extends sets up the inheritance chain between classes.
super(name) calls the parent constructor — required before using this.
Override methods by redefining them in the child class.
Add new methods that the parent doesn't have.

practice.task: Create a Vehicle base class with start() and stop() methods. Create a Truck subclass that overrides start() to add a cargo check, and adds a load() method.

keyTakeaways: extends creates an inheritance relationship between classes.
super() must be called in the child constructor before using this.
Override parent methods by redefining them in the child class.
super.method() lets you call the parent's version when overriding.
lessons.challenge: Build a 3-level class hierarchy: Shape → Polygon → Rectangle. Each level adds properties and overrides a describe() method.
